title: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
summary: Documents the format commonly used for Comma-Separated Values files and registers the text/csv MIME type. It describes the common practice rather than defining a new standard. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A CSV file is a table written as plain lines, with commas between the boxes. This memo writes down how those files usually look and gives them an official name for the internet.

questions: what is the text/csv mime type
how do you escape quotes in csv
subtitle: Writes down how comma-separated values files usually look and registers text/csv as their MIME type.

tldr.problem: CSV files were widely used to move data between spreadsheet programs, but the format was never formally documented and no MIME type had been registered for it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records the format most implementations seem to follow (one record per line, fields split by commas, double quotes for special characters), gives an ABNF grammar, and registers text/csv with optional charset and header parameters.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and describes common practice rather than a standard. Real-world files still vary, so implementations are told to be conservative in what they send and liberal in what they accept.

today: RFC 4180 is Informational and is updated by RFC 7111. It records common practice rather than defining a standard.

sections.title: Why CSV Needed Writing Down
sections.content:
The comma separated values (CSV) format has been used for exchanging and converting data between spreadsheet programs for quite some time. Surprisingly, the RFC says, it had never been formally documented.

There was also a gap in the MIME registry: IANA already had text/tab-separated-values, but nothing for CSV, and various programs and operating systems had started using different MIME types for it. RFC 4180 documents the format and registers text/csv in accordance with the registration procedures of RFC 2048.
sections.eli5: Lots of programs saved tables in the same simple style, but nobody had ever written the rules down or given the style an official name. This memo does both.

sections.title: The Seven Rules of the CSV Format
sections.content:
The RFC admits there is no formal specification, which allows a wide variety of interpretations. Section 2 therefore records the format that seems to be followed by most implementations, as seven rules.

  • Each record sits on its own line, ended by a line break (CRLF). The last record may or may not have an ending line break.
  • An optional header line may come first, in the same format as the other lines. It should have the same number of fields as the records.
  • Fields are separated by commas. Each line should contain the same number of fields, spaces are part of a field, and the last field must not be followed by a comma.
  • Fields may or may not be enclosed in double quotes. If they are not, double quotes may not appear inside them.
  • Fields containing line breaks, double quotes or commas should be enclosed in double quotes.
  • Inside a quoted field, a double quote is escaped by preceding it with another double quote.

The RFC also gives an ABNF grammar: a file is an optional header, then one or more records separated by CRLF, with an optional final CRLF. A field is either escaped (in double quotes) or non-escaped.
sections.eli5: Each row of the table goes on its own line and the boxes in a row are split with commas. If a box itself has a comma or a quote mark in it, you wrap the box in quote marks, and write a quote inside it twice.

sections.title: Quoting in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates the rules with short examples. A header line looks like field_name,field_name,field_name followed by ordinary records such as aaa,bbb,ccc.

A field that contains a line break must be quoted, so one record can span two lines, and a quote inside a quoted field is doubled, as in "aaa","b""bb","ccc". The RFC also notes that some programs, such as Microsoft Excel, do not use double quotes at all.
sections.eli5: Quote marks work like a fence around a box. Everything inside the fence belongs to that box, even commas. To put a quote mark inside the fence, you write it twice.

sections.title: The text/csv MIME Type
sections.content:
Section 3 is the media-type registration application. The type is text, the subtype is csv, and no parameters are required. Two are optional: charset and header.

The common character set for CSV is US-ASCII, but other character sets defined by IANA for the text tree may be used with the charset parameter. The header parameter says whether a header line is present, with valid values present or absent. Implementors who do not use it must decide for themselves whether the header is there.

As for line breaks, the type uses CRLF, although some implementations may use other values. The listed uses are spreadsheet programs and data conversion utilities, the file extension is CSV, and the author and change controller is the IESG. Section 4 records that IANA registered the type.
sections.eli5: The memo gives CSV files an official label, text/csv, like a name tag. The label can also say which alphabet the file uses and whether the first line is a row of titles.

sections.title: Interoperability and Its Limits
sections.content:
The registration is frank that, because there is no single specification, there are considerable differences among implementations. It points to the definition in Section 2 as an attempt at a common one, and says there is no single master specification for the format.

Implementors are advised to "be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others", a quotation the RFC attributes to RFC 793, when processing CSV files.
sections.eli5: Because everyone made up their own version, files can differ. The advice is to write neat files yourself and to be patient when reading other people's messy ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says CSV files contain passive text data that should not pose any risks. It adds that, in theory, malicious binary data could be included to exploit potential buffer overruns in the program that processes the CSV data.

It also notes that private data may be shared via this format, which it says applies to any text data. Section 5 of the RFC simply refers back to this discussion.
sections.eli5: A CSV file is just plain writing, so it is usually safe. But a sneaky file could try to confuse a careless program, and the table might hold private information.

data.title: CSV grammar
data.code:
file = [header CRLF] record *(CRLF record) [CRLF]
header = name *(COMMA name)
record = field *(COMMA field)
name = field
field = (escaped / non-escaped)
escaped = DQUOTE *(TEXTDATA / COMMA / CR / LF / 2DQUOTE) DQUOTE
non-escaped = *TEXTDATA
COMMA = %x2C
CR = %x0D
DQUOTE = %x22
LF = %x0A
CRLF = CR LF
TEXTDATA = %x20-21 / %x23-2B / %x2D-7E
